screens.title: Consuming RESTful APIs
screens.subtitle: Connect Flutter apps to web services with HTTP, JSON, and async UI patterns

narration.text: In mobile apps, most dynamic features come from remote services. In this lesson you will learn what a RESTful A P I is, how to use Flutter's http package to make requests, and how to convert JSON into usable Dart objects. We'll also practice integrating asynchronous results into the UI with FutureBuilder and explore common error cases you must defend against. As a concrete example, we'll fetch lists of posts and users from a test A P I, parse them into model classes, and display them safely in a ListView. You will see how GET retrieves data, how POST sends JSON in the request body, and how status codes signal success or failure. Finally, we'll cover practical mistakes beginners make — like forgetting to await a future or not checking status codes — and show how to present friendly messages to users when network problems occur. By the end of this chapter you will be able to fetch, send, and display A P I data in a Flutter app and know where to add error checks and user feedback. Think about a simple app that shows user profiles — how would you show a loading state and handle a timeout?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: APIs let your app fetch live data and send user changes. Mastering HTTP requests and JSON handling is essential for real-world Flutter apps.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives define the practical skills you'll practice. First, you will explain core REST concepts and why HTTP verbs matter when interacting with resources. Second, you will use Flutter's http package to make GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE requests, sending and receiving data safely. Third, you will convert JSON into Dart objects and serialize Dart objects into JSON for network exchange, which prevents runtime type errors and eases UI binding. Fourth, you will integrate asynchronous results into widgets using FutureBuilder and design friendly error states for network failures. Each objective focuses on application: knowing the theory is not enough — you'll construct working fetch and send functions, parse nested JSON like a user's address city, and present loading and error states. These skills are central for building apps that rely on remote data, because they keep the UI responsive and robust when networks are unreliable. Think of these objectives as the checklist for a small feature: fetch a list of users, show them, and handle failures gracefully.

screens.title: What is a RESTful API?
screens.subtitle: Resource-based services using standard HTTP verbs

narration.text: A RESTful A P I is an architectural style that models server data as resources and uses standard HTTP methods to operate on them. In practice this means you address data with URIs, and you use verbs like GET to retrieve a resource, POST to create one, PUT to update, and DELETE to remove it. The key point is semantics: using the right verb communicates intent to intermediaries and to other developers, which affects caching, security, and expected responses. For example, a GET on /posts returns a collection or a single post and should be safe and side-effect free. A POST to /posts creates a new post and usually returns 201 Created with the new entity. A common misconception is treating all network calls as the same; in reality, a bad verb choice can break idempotency and lead to duplicate data or unexpected side effects. Consider a simple app that lists posts: you want GET for retrieving items and POST only when the user submits a new post. Understanding these rules makes your client-server interactions more predictable and compatible with other services. How would you design the URL and verb choices for a comments feature?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: REST maps resources to URIs and uses HTTP verbs for CRUD semantics; correct verb use matters for expected behavior and interoperability.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What is a RESTful API?
RESTful API — core idea
Model server data as resources and operate via HTTP verbs with predictable semantics.
GET: retrieve without side effects (safe)
POST: create new resource; often returns 201
PUT: update or replace an existing resource
DELETE: remove a resource
Example & Analogy
Analogy: think of resources as files. GET reads a file, POST creates a new file, PUT overwrites a file, and DELETE removes it. Using the correct verb prevents accidental overwrites and clarifies intent.
Concrete Example
GET https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts returns a list of posts. POST to the same endpoint with JSON creates a new post and typically returns a 201 status.
Key Takeaway
Correct HTTP semantics make APIs predictable and safe for clients and servers.

screens.title: Comparing GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
screens.subtitle: When to use each method and what responses to expect

narration.text: HTTP provides a small set of verbs that map cleanly to CRUD operations. GET retrieves a resource and should be safe and idempotent; repeated GETs do not change server state. POST creates resources and is not idempotent — calling POST twice may create two records; servers commonly return 201 Created with the new object. PUT replaces or updates a resource and is idempotent: calling PUT multiple times with the same body should result in the same server state. DELETE removes a resource and should also be idempotent in intent. Understanding idempotency helps you design retry strategies: if a request fails, retrying a PUT is generally safe, retrying a POST might create duplicates. Concrete example: creating a post requires POST to /posts with a JSON body and the Content-Type header set to application/json; updating an existing post uses PUT to /posts/1. A common mistake is using GET for operations that alter state; that breaks expectations and caching. Think in terms of resource identity and whether repeated requests must be safe to repeat without unintended side effects. Comparing GET, POST, PUT, DELETE means get=read, post=create, put=update/replace, delete=remove. consider idempotency when designing retries and client behavior.. In practical terms, when to use each method and what responses to expect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Method Comparison
keyIdea.text: GET=read, POST=create, PUT=update/replace, DELETE=remove. Consider idempotency when designing retries and client behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Comparing HTTP Methods
Method Summary
GET
Retrieve data. Safe and cacheable. Expect 200 OK for successful responses.
POST
Create new resources. Not idempotent. Expect 201 Created on success.
PUT
Update or replace a resource. Idempotent; repeated requests produce same result.
DELETE
Remove a resource. Idempotent intent; check server behavior for soft deletes or responses.
Practical guidance
If you plan to retry failed requests automatically, prefer idempotent methods. For create operations, implement server-side deduplication if clients may retry POST requests.
Example
To update post 1: PUT https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1 with a JSON body representing the new values. Server should respond with 200 or 204.
Key Takeaway

Match verbs to intent. Decide retry behavior based on idempotency.

screens.title: Using the http package: GET example
screens.subtitle: Add the package, fetch posts, and parse JSON into models

narration.text: The http package is the simplest tool for HTTP in Flutter. First, add it to pubspec. yaml and run the package manager. In code, import dart:convert for json decoding and import package:http/http. dart as http to avoid name collisions. The core pattern is: build a Uri, await http. get, check response. statusCode, and then jsonDecode the response body. Convert the resulting list or map into model objects via a factory constructor. A common pitfall is not checking the status code before decoding: decoding an error page or empty body leads to runtime exceptions. Another mistake is performing network calls synchronously; always use async and await so the UI remains responsive. Concrete example: a Post model with id, title, and body and a fetchPosts function that returns Future >. In the UI, call fetchPosts in initState and store the Future in a field so FutureBuilder can consume it. This pattern separates networking from UI logic and makes testing easier. How will you validate keys inside fromJson to avoid FormatException? Using the http package: GET example means build a uri, await http.get, check status code, jsondecode the body, then map to typed model objects.. In practical terms, add the package, fetch posts, and parse json into models. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: GET Pattern
keyIdea.text: Build a Uri, await http.get, check status code, jsonDecode the body, then map to typed model objects.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › GET example
Code Walkthrough
A compact example shows the exact pattern used in apps.
import 'dart:convert';
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

class Post {
  final int id;
  final String title;
  final String body;

  Post({required this.id, required this.title, required this.body});

  factory Post.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) {
    return Post(
      id: json['id'],
      title: json['title'],
      body: json['body'],
    );
  }
}

Future<List<Post>> fetchPosts() async {
  final response = await http.get(Uri.parse('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts'));
  if (response.statusCode == 200) {
    final List<dynamic> jsonList = jsonDecode(response.body);
    return jsonList.map((j) => Post.fromJson(j)).toList();
  } else {
    throw Exception('Failed to load posts: ${response.statusCode}');
  }
}
Explanation
  • Import dart:convert and alias the http package to avoid conflicts.
  • Await the network call and check response.statusCode before decoding.
  • jsonDecode returns List or Map depending on the payload; map to strong types promptly.
Concrete Example
Use fetchPosts() in initState and provide the Future to FutureBuilder so the UI reacts to connection states automatically.
Key Takeaway

Check status codes before decoding and convert JSON to model objects to keep UI code clean.

screens.title: Parsing JSON into models
screens.subtitle: Design factory constructors and access nested fields safely

narration.text: Correctly parsing JSON into Dart model objects prevents many runtime errors. Start by inspecting the JSON shape: for a user object, you might have nested address data where address. city is inside another map. Your factory constructor should access nested maps carefully and validate expected keys when appropriate. For example, build a User model with id, name, email, and a city field derived from json['address']['city']. A common error is assuming nested keys always exist; protect code with casts or null checks where the A P I may omit fields. For larger models or many models, consider generated serializers, but for this chapter we will write manual factory methods to show the mechanics. Also avoid tight coupling between networking and model creation: keep fetch functions responsible for HTTP and factories responsible for mapping. This separation helps testing since you can unit test fromJson behavior with sample JSON. Concrete example: implement a User. fromJson that extracts city from the nested address map. A quick test is to decode a small sample JSON string and ensure the produced user has the city you expect.

keyIdea.title: Modeling JSON
keyIdea.text: Write clear factory constructors that map nested JSON fields to flattened model properties and guard against missing keys.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Parsing JSON into models
User Model Example
Access nested keys and return a simple, testable object shape.
class User {
  final int id;
  final String name;
  final String email;
  final String city;

  User({required this.id, required this.name, required this.email, required this.city});

  factory User.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) {
    final address = json['address'] as Map<String, dynamic>;
    return User(
      id: json['id'],
      name: json['name'],
      email: json['email'],
      city: address['city'],
    );
  }
}
Guidelines
  • Inspect the JSON structure and map nested objects explicitly.
  • Use casts like as Map<String, dynamic> to safely work with nested objects.
  • Guard against missing keys to avoid FormatException; consider default values.
Test Tip
Write small unit tests that call User.fromJson with sample JSON to validate behavior when fields are missing or types differ.
Key Takeaway

Keep parsing logic explicit and test factories with sample JSON to catch format issues early.

screens.title: Integrating FutureBuilder
screens.subtitle: Show loading, error, and data states without blocking the UI

narration.text: FutureBuilder is the recommended widget for wiring a single Future into your widget tree. The pattern is straightforward: start the fetch in initState and store the Future in a field. Pass that Future to FutureBuilder so the builder callback receives snapshots as the Future progresses. The snapshot has connectionState values: waiting for in-progress operations, done when complete. Additionally snapshot. hasError and snapshot. hasData let you selectively render a loading spinner, an error message, or your data. A frequent beginner mistake is calling the fetch function directly inside build, causing repeated requests on every rebuild. Storing the future once avoids that. Also separate concerns: keep networking in a repository or service, models in their files, and UI in its widget. Concrete UI behavior: when waiting, show CircularProgressIndicator; when hasError, display a friendly message and retry hint; when hasData, render ListView. builder using the typed list. A quick thought experiment: how would you show a pull-to-refresh while still using the same FutureBuilder pattern? Integrating FutureBuilder means create and store the future in initstate, pass it to futurebuilder, and render loading, error, or data states using snapshot properties.. In practical terms, show loading, error, and data states without blocking the ui. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: FutureBuilder Pattern
keyIdea.text: Create and store the Future in initState, pass it to FutureBuilder, and render loading, error, or data states using snapshot properties.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Integrating FutureBuilder
FutureBuilder Essentials
Start the Future once, then let FutureBuilder render snapshots.
// in State class
Future<List<Post>>? _postsFuture;

@override
void initState() {
  super.initState();
  _postsFuture = fetchPosts();
}

// in build
FutureBuilder<List<Post>>(
  future: _postsFuture,
  builder: (context, snapshot) {
    if (snapshot.connectionState == ConnectionState.waiting) {
      return Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());
    } else if (snapshot.hasError) {
      return Center(child: Text('Error: ${snapshot.error}'));
    } else if (snapshot.hasData) {
      final posts = snapshot.data!;
      return ListView.builder(...);
    } else {
      return Center(child: Text('No data found.'));
    }
  },
)
Best Practices
  • Initialize the Future once in initState to avoid repeated network calls.
  • Provide user-friendly error messages and consider retry strategies.
  • Keep UI logic separate from networking code for testability.
Concrete Example
Use FutureBuilder to switch between a CircularProgressIndicator, an error text, or a ListView.builder once data arrives.

screens.title: Making POST requests
screens.subtitle: Encode Dart maps to JSON and set headers correctly

narration.text: Sending data to a server requires encoding Dart structures as JSON and signaling the format via headers. Use jsonEncode to convert a Dart map into a JSON string and set the Content-Type header to application/json; charset=UTF-8. When you call http. post with this body, the server usually returns 201 Created and may include the created resource in the response. Always check for a 201 status code rather than assuming success. Another practical point is to avoid sending Dart types that jsonEncode cannot serialize directly; convert DateTimes or custom objects to strings or numbers explicitly before encoding. You will also practice handling the response — decode the response body and construct a model object representing the created item. A common misconception is that a null or empty response body implies success; instead rely on status codes and documented A P I behavior. For testing, the JSONPlaceholder A P I returns a resource representation so you can inspect the created object's fields. Consider how you would show success feedback in the UI and clear form inputs after a successful create. Making POST requests means use jsonencode on a dart map, set content-type to application/json, and check for 201 created before parsing the response.. In practical terms, encode dart maps to json and set headers correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: POST Pattern
keyIdea.text: Use jsonEncode on a Dart map, set Content-Type to application/json, and check for 201 Created before parsing the response.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Making POST requests
POST Example
Encode the request body and set headers correctly.
Future<Post> createPost(String title, String body) async {
  final response = await http.post(
    Uri.parse('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts'),
    headers: <String, String>{
      'Content-Type': 'application/json; charset=UTF-8',
    },
    body: jsonEncode(<String, String>{
      'title': title,
      'body': body,
      'userId': '1',
    }),
  );

  if (response.statusCode == 201) {
    return Post.fromJson(jsonDecode(response.body));
  } else {
    throw Exception('Failed to create post: ${response.statusCode}');
  }
}
Notes & Tips
  • Always set the Content-Type header when sending JSON.
  • Check for 201 Created on success and decode the response into a model.
  • Sanitize and validate data client-side before sending to avoid server errors.
Common Mistake
Sending a Dart Map directly as body will result in form-encoded data rather than JSON. Use jsonEncode to produce a proper JSON string.

screens.title: Handling Network Errors
screens.subtitle: Catch exceptions, check status codes, and present friendly UI

narration.text: Network requests fail for many reasons: lost connectivity, timeouts, server errors, or malformed responses. Effective error handling expects these failures and responds with clear user feedback. Wrap http calls in try-catch blocks and catch broad exceptions like SocketException or TimeoutException when possible. Always inspect response. statusCode: codes like 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found, or 500 Internal Server Error indicate different problems and should produce tailored messages or flows. For example, a 401 might prompt re-authentication, while 404 suggests the requested resource no longer exists. Avoid exposing raw exception text directly to users; instead log details for developers and show concise, actionable messages to users. Implement retry policies for transient errors and consider exponential backoff rather than immediate repeated requests. A common misuse is assuming any non-200 status is permanent; for connectivity issues, a retry with backoff may solve temporary failures. Finally, design the UI so users can retry operations manually and understand whether data is stale or missing. Handling Network Errors means use try-catch to handle exceptions, check status codes for specific responses, and provide clear user messaging plus retry options.. In practical terms, catch exceptions, check status codes, and present friendly ui. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Error Strategy
keyIdea.text: Use try-catch to handle exceptions, check status codes for specific responses, and provide clear user messaging plus retry options.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Handling Network Errors
Common error types
  • Connectivity: SocketException when device is offline.
  • Timeouts: Server too slow; use timeouts and backoff.
  • Status codes: 4xx and 5xx errors require different responses.
  • Format errors: malformed JSON causing FormatException.
Example
Wrap calls in try-catch and display a retry button after logging details for debugging. For unauthorized responses, guide the user to sign in again.
Retry & Backoff
For transient failures use exponential backoff. Avoid immediate repeated retries which can worsen server load or cause duplicate operations for non-idempotent methods.
Key Takeaway

Differentiate between connectivity, server, and parsing errors. Log details, inform users clearly, and design safe retry strategies.

screens.title: PUT and DELETE examples
screens.subtitle: Update and remove resources with expected semantics

narration.text: PUT and DELETE are the primary verbs for updating and removing resources. When updating, use PUT and include the full representation you want the server to hold; many APIs accept partial updates via PATCH but PUT typically replaces the resource. For example, updating post 1 involves sending a PUT to /posts/1 with a JSON body holding the new title and body. Check for 200 OK or 204 No Content depending on A P I behavior. For delete operations use DELETE to /posts/1 and expect a 200, 202, or 204 response on success. A subtle point is idempotency: repeated PUT or DELETE calls should leave the server in the same state, so they are safe for retries. However, verify server semantics because some implementations perform soft deletes or return different status codes. Always handle responses and inform the user: on successful delete remove the item from the UI, on update refresh the displayed data. A common pitfall is ignoring the server response and assuming the local state matches server-side state; prefer to update local state after confirming the network operation succeeded.

keyIdea.title: PUT & DELETE
keyIdea.text: Use PUT to replace or update a resource and DELETE to remove one; check responses and update UI only after confirming success.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › PUT & DELETE examples
PUT Example
final response = await http.put(
  Uri.parse('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1'),
  headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json; charset=UTF-8'},
  body: jsonEncode({'id': 1, 'title': newTitle, 'body': newBody}),
);
if (response.statusCode == 200) {
  // parse updated object or refresh list
} else {
  throw Exception('Failed to update: ${response.statusCode}');
}
DELETE Example
final response = await http.delete(
  Uri.parse('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1'),
);
if (response.statusCode == 200 || response.statusCode == 204) {
  // remove item from UI
} else {
  throw Exception('Failed to delete: ${response.statusCode}');
}
Key Takeaway

Confirm server responses before changing local UI state; repeated PUT/DELETE should be safe to retry if server respects idempotency.

screens.title: Security, performance, and production notes
screens.subtitle: Avoid hardcoded secrets, prefer HTTPS, and design for scale

narration.text: When moving from prototype to production there are a few important concerns. Never hardcode A P I keys or secrets in your code; instead use environment variables or a secure keystore approach provided by the platform. Always use HTTPS to protect data over the network. Consider caching strategies for frequently fetched data to reduce latency and conserve mobile bandwidth. For large lists use pagination or lazy loading rather than fetching massive result sets in a single request. When parsing JSON, validate types and lengths to avoid crashes from unexpected payloads. Implement graceful degradation: if the network is slow, show cached state and indicate freshness. Monitor status codes and log errors for debugging, but keep user messages concise and actionable. A frequent misconception is that adding more retries always improves reliability; without backoff retries can overload slow servers. Finally, document the A P I contracts you rely on so teams can coordinate changes without breaking clients. Security, performance, and production notes means use secure storage for secrets, prefer https, cache sensibly, paginate large results, and use retries with backoff to avoid overloading services.. keyIdea.title: Production Readiness
keyIdea.text: Use secure storage for secrets, prefer HTTPS, cache sensibly, paginate large results, and use retries with backoff to avoid overloading services.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Production notes
Security & Performance
Never check in API keys. Use environment or secure keystore solutions. Prefer HTTPS for all endpoints.
Cache responses where appropriate and use pagination for large lists to reduce data usage and improve perceived performance.
Use retries with exponential backoff for transient errors; avoid aggressive immediate retries.
Developer practices
  • Log network errors for diagnostics but avoid verbose messages in the UI.
  • Document API contracts and versions to reduce breaking changes.
  • Validate JSON shapes and handle unexpected fields gracefully.
Key Takeaway

Design for security, efficiency, and resilience before shipping networked features to real users.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the core ideas to carry forward. First: RESTful APIs treat server data as resources and use HTTP verbs to convey intent; choose verbs carefully to preserve semantics. Second: The http package is a simple, effective client for Flutter; always await responses and check status codes before decoding. Third: JSON must be decoded into typed Dart models; write factory constructors that handle nested objects and validate keys to avoid format errors. Fourth: FutureBuilder lets you integrate asynchronous results into the UI cleanly, showing loading, error, and data states without blocking the main thread. Fifth: Implement robust error handling and retry strategies, and never hardcode secrets or use unencrypted endpoints in production. These concepts are practical: they map directly to tasks such as fetching posts, posting new records, updating items, and deleting them while keeping the UI responsive and users informed. Use this checklist as you implement your next networked feature.

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: 3 compact reminders to use while coding

narration.text: Keep three practical reminders at hand while you develop networked features. First, always check response. statusCode and never assume success; use 200 for GET, 201 for resource creation, and consult A P I docs for other codes. Second, convert JSON into typed Dart models with factory constructors and guard against missing or malformed fields to avoid runtime crashes. Third, wire asynchronous results into the UI with FutureBuilder and avoid calling network functions directly inside build; start futures in initState or in response to explicit user actions. These simple checks prevent common bugs and keep your UI responsive and robust while your app interacts with remote services. Use them as a short checklist during development and testing.
